1:---
2:name: versioning
3:description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
4:---
5:
6:# Versioning
7:
8:How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
9:branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
10:things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.
11:
12:## 1. Repositories
13:
14:A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
15:repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
16:inside it.
17:
18:| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
19:|---|---|---|
20:| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
21:| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |
22:
23:`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
24:and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
25:codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
26:in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
27:submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
28:mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
29:`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.
30:
31:A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
32:in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
33:[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.
34:
35:An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.
36:
37:## 2. Branches
38:
39:| branch | name | checked out |
40:|---|---|---|
41:| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
42:| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
43:| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
44:| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
45:| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
46:| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |
47:
48:The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
49:user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
50:`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
51:campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
52:the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.
53:
54:A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
55:it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
56:have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
57:`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
58:another, so no two module branches collide.
59:
60:A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
61:a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
62:fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.
63:
64:An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
65:way.
66:
67:## 3. Worktrees
68:
69:Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
70:`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
71:[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
72:module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
73:`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
74:planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.
75:
76:## 4. Landing
77:
78:A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
79:out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
80:no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
81:subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
82:objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
83:and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
84:`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
85:and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
86:progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
87:repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
88:[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.
89:
90:The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
91:the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
92:update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
93:enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.
94:
95:### 4.1 The landing lock
96:
97:An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
98:exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
99:`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:
100:
101:```text
102:$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
103:```
104:
105:A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
106:until its landing has succeeded:
107:
108:1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
109:2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
110:   lands while it holds the lock;
111:3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
112:   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
113:   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
114:4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
115:5. it releases the lock.
116:
117:A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
118:that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.
119:
120:The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
121:and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
122:its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
123:CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
124:that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
125:holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
126:and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
127:and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
128:walking up the shell's parent processes:
129:<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
130:documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->
131:
132:```bash
133:lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
134:mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
135:# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
136:sh -c '
137:  exec 9>"$1"
138:  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
139:  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
140:' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
141:# release, once the push has succeeded
142:holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
143:```
144:
145:The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
146:that a release never removes the next holder's record.
147:
148:The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
149:stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
150:agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
151:running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
152:record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.
153:
154:### 4.2 Commits
155:
156:Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
157:commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
158:base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
159:neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
160:become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.
161:
162:The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
163:pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
164:describes.
165:<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
166:remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
167:it. -->
168:
169:### 4.3 Promotion
170:
171:A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
172:branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
173:through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.
174:
175:### 4.4 Progress
176:
177:The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
178:campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
179:its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
180:`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.
181:
182:### 4.5 Integration
183:
184:A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
185:last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
186:it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
187:other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
188:record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.
189:
190:1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
191:   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
192:   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
193:   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
194:   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
195:   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
196:   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
197:   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
198:   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
199:2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
200:   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
201:   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
202:   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
203:   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
204:   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
205:   over are listed before its C tests leave.
206:3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.
207:
208:Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
209:one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
210:their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
211:the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.
212:
213:## 5. Lifecycle
214:
215:Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
216:only it needed is purged.
217:
218:### 5.1 Campaign
219:
220:The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
221:the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
222:until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.
223:
224:The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
225:it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
226:the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
227:[Progress](#44-progress) describes.
228:
229:### 5.2 Planner runs
230:
231:A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
232:branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.
233:
234:### 5.3 Modules
235:
236:A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
237:the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.
238:
239:A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
240:once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
241:whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
242:consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
243:[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
244:from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
245:module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
246:its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
247:are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.
248:
249:### 5.4 Waves
250:
251:A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
252:later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
253:before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
254:requires; that commit is the wave's base.
255:Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
256:describes, and its branch purged.
257:
258:A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
259:they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.
260:
261:### 5.5 Batches
262:
263:A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
264:launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
265:not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
266:and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
267:records, since no batch changes the C.
268:Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
269:recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
270:[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
271:inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.
272:
273:## 6. Identity
274:
275:Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
276:as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
277:`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
278:unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
279:as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
280:message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
281:agent's host suggests included.
282:
283:The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
284:that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
285:host may have no git identity of its own.

53:
54:A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
55:it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
56:have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
57:`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
58:another, so no two module branches collide.
59:
60:A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
61:a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
62:fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.
63:
64:An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
65:way.
66:
67:## 3. Worktrees
68:
69:Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
70:`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
71:[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
72:module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
73:`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
74:planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.
75:
76:## 4. Landing
77:
78:A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
79:out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
80:no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
81:subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
82:objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
83:and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
84:`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
85:and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
86:progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
87:repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
88:[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.
89:
90:The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
91:the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
92:update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
93:enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.
94:
95:### 4.1 The landing lock
96:
97:An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
98:exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
99:`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:
100:
101:```text
102:$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
103:```
104:
105:A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
106:until its landing has succeeded:
107:
108:1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
109:2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
110:   lands while it holds the lock;
111:3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
112:   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
113:   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
114:4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
115:5. it releases the lock.
116:
117:A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
118:that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.
119:
120:The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
121:and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
122:its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
123:CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
124:that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
125:holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
126:and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
127:and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
128:walking up the shell's parent processes:
129:<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
130:documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->
131:
132:```bash
133:lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
134:mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
135:# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
136:sh -c '
137:  exec 9>"$1"
138:  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
139:  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
140:' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
141:# release, once the push has succeeded
142:holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
143:```
144:
145:The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
146:that a release never removes the next holder's record.
147:
148:The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
149:stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
150:agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
151:running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
152:record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.
153:
154:### 4.2 Commits
155:
156:Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
157:commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
158:base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
159:neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
160:become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.
161:
162:The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
163:pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
164:describes.
165:<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
166:remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
167:it. -->
168:
169:### 4.3 Promotion
170:
171:A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
172:branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
173:through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.
174:
175:### 4.4 Progress
176:
177:The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
178:campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
179:its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
180:`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.
181:
182:### 4.5 Integration
183:
184:A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
185:last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
186:it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
187:other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
188:record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.
189:
190:1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
191:   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
192:   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
193:   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
194:   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
195:   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
196:   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
197:   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
198:   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
199:2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
200:   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
201:   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
202:   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
203:   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
204:   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
205:   over are listed before its C tests leave.
206:3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.
207:
208:Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
209:one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
210:their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
211:the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.
212:
213:## 5. Lifecycle
214:
215:Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
216:only it needed is purged.
217:
218:### 5.1 Campaign
219:
220:The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
221:the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
222:until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.
223:
224:The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
225:it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
226:the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
227:[Progress](#44-progress) describes.
228:
229:### 5.2 Planner runs
230:
231:A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
232:branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.
233:
234:### 5.3 Modules
235:
236:A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
237:the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.
238:
239:A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
240:once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
241:whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
242:consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
243:[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
244:from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
245:module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
246:its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
247:are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.
248:
249:### 5.4 Waves
250:
251:A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
252:later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
253:before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
254:requires; that commit is the wave's base.
255:Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
256:describes, and its branch purged.
257:
258:A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
259:they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.
260:
261:### 5.5 Batches
262:
263:A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
264:launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
265:not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
266:and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
267:records, since no batch changes the C.
268:Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
269:recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
270:[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
271:inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.
272:
273:## 6. Identity
274:
275:Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
276:as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
277:`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
278:unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
279:as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
280:message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
281:agent's host suggests included.
282:
283:The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
284:that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
285:host may have no git identity of its own.

---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 4: the lifecycle, the name functions and the dispatchers

api.c's last `port` batch, the `symbol` route of waves 195 and 196: 32 items in
`src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`. `fn::llhttp_init` is `ParserMut::init(ParserType,
Option<SettingsRef<'static>>)`, over `reinit`, `set_parser_type` and `set_settings`;
`fn::llhttp_reset` is `ParserMut::reset()`, which keeps the type byte, the table, `data` and the
lenient flags across `reinit`, so a parser of both kinds keeps the type its first message
settled; `fn::llhttp_finish` is `ParserMut::finish() -> Result<(), FinishError>`, where
`FinishError` is `InvalidEofState` (with C's reason `"Invalid EOF state"`) or
`on_message_complete`'s own non-zero value, `HPE_PAUSED` included, neither kept as the parser's
error, as C keeps neither. A parser with an error finishes at once, as C's does, and a finish
state no `llhttp_finish` names panics where C aborts. `fn::llhttp_settings_init` keeps batch 2's
`Settings::new()`, now native, the zeroed table its `memset` leaves; its anchor moved from
`Wraps` to `Replaces`. The name functions `llhttp_errno_name`, `llhttp_method_name` and
`llhttp_status_name` are each a `switch` of the cases batch 3's generators stand for, so they
are ported onto `Errno::constant_name`, `Method::map_string` and `Status::map_string`, which
carry a third anchor each (`crustify/evolution/port-onto-an-existing-accessor`, with this
evidence); their `default: abort()` no enum reaches.

The 23 dispatchers are one table, `with_dispatchers!`, from which the native methods, the
region's slot reads and the gateway's exports are made. `mac::CALLBACK_MAYBE` and
`mac::SPAN_CALLBACK_MAYBE` are the private `callback_maybe(EventSlot)` and
`span_callback_maybe(SpanSlot, &[u8])`, the stringified `#NAME` a per-slot `&'static CStr` made
at compile time; each `fn::llhttp__on_<slot>` is the public `ParserMut::on_<slot>()` or
`on_<slot>(&[u8])` over them, returning C's `int`, which `llhttp.c`'s port will call. A
dispatcher reads the table the parser holds through `ffi_import` alone: the region maps a slot

`src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`. `fn::llhttp__internal_init` is `Parser::new` (and
`Default`), the safe constructor batch 0 left, and `ParserMut::reinit` in place, which
`llhttp_init` and `llhttp_reset` start from; its `init` role in the ownership store holds
against its body (`memset`, then the start state). `fn::llhttp__internal_execute` is
`ParserMut::parse(&[u8]) -> Result<Parsed, ParseError>`, the run's start and end one slice:
`HPE_OK` and the two resumable pauses are `Parsed`, since libgit2's `httpparser.c` treats
them as an early stop, and any other code, an `llhttp_errno` or a data callback's own value,
is a `ParseError` the parser keeps. The names leave api.c's own (`init`, `reset`,
`execute`) to its port. Two C behaviours are refused rather than carried: a parser with no
state to run from (`_current` is `s_error`, 0, with no error, as `Parser::zeroed()` or a
parser cleared after `HPE_PAUSED_H2_UPGRADE` leaves it) reaches `abort()`, and a callback
that executes or initialises the parser whose execute runs it corrupts the outer run (a span
pointing into the nested input, `_index` past a match sequence). `parse` panics on the
first, and `parse` and `reinit` on the second through a thread-local register of the parsers
each thread is executing, which the trampolines' barrier turns into the callback's error
(`crustify/evolution/callback-reenters-its-caller`).

`fnp::llhttp_cb` and `fnp::llhttp_data_cb` are `Callback` and `DataCallback`, a function
pointer each, `Copy` and never released: neither has a context parameter, the parser's
`data` being the context, so a Rust implementation is a stateless `EventHandler` or
`DataHandler` type reached through a trampoline behind `callback::barrier` (`-1` on a panic,
a NULL parser or a NULL run), as `trace.rs`'s `git_trace_cb` is. The C form is a
`pub(crate)` `unsafe` constructor, whose contract no C callback that reads `data` meets;
such a callback is reached through the settings its parser runs with
(`crustify/evolution/callback-context-in-an-argument`). `call` is safe, and `raw` gives the
slot value a settings table holds, which api.c's `llhttp_settings_s` binds next.
`mac::HTTP_ERRNO_MAP`, `mac::HTTP_ALL_METHOD_MAP` and `mac::HTTP_STATUS_MAP` are the enums'
own tables, not a second one: their entries are batch 0's variants in the enums' order,
which the X-macros share. Each of `Errno`, `Method` and `Status` gains `MAP`, `map_name`
(`NAME`), `map_string` (`STRING`) and `constant_name` (`PREFIX##NAME`, the case label, and
`llhttp_errno_name`'s text), each a `&'static CStr` sliced at compile time from the
stringified bindgen constant; `llhttp_enum!` takes the one `STRING` that differs,
`M-SEARCH`, beside its variant, and checks every prefix at compile time. They are
`Replaces`, so the three count as ported symbols, the four others as wrapped.

The raw bindings gain the two functions, the two callback types and, for the equivalence
tests, api.c's `llhttp_errno_name`, `llhttp_method_name` and `llhttp_status_name`. The
ownership store gains the pointer findings of `llhttp__internal_execute` (the run's
pointers retained in `_span_pos0` and `error_pos` and never followed after the call) and of
the two callback types. Tests: 17 `unit_pub` (the maps' columns and order, the parse in
every run size, pauses, upgrade, the kept error, the two panics, the callbacks and their
panics), 7 `ub_safe` (runs freed between parses, parsers moved mid-message, runs at the
edges of their allocations, handlers called from Rust that parse and initialise, callbacks
across threads), 8 `ub_unsafe` in `set_settings_ptr`'s suite (Rust handlers C calls through
the trampolines: runs in every size, a pause, a handler's own code, a panic, the refused
re-entry and re-initialisation, a nested parse of another parser), 5 `equiv` (the maps
against `llhttp.h`'s text and api.c's three name functions; `new` and `reinit` byte for byte
against `llhttp__internal_init`, private state included; `parse` against
`llhttp__internal_execute` by outcome, whole parser and handler calls after every run), 7
doctests and 2 compile-fail doctests (a handler sending its parser to another thread, a
callable built from a bare C function). llhttp has no C tests in the tree.

### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 2: `llhttp_settings_s`, the callback table

api.c's one type, wrapped ahead of its `port` waves in its own file,
`src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`: `st::llhttp_settings_s` is `Settings`, a `define_ctype!`
layout with `SettingsRef` and `SettingsMut`, kept in its C layout until its `port/layout`
(wave 1165), since libgit2's `transports/httpclient.c` fills a `static` table in C and hands
it to `llhttp_init`. Its typedefs `llhttp_settings_t` and `git_http_parser_settings` are the
aliases `SettingsT` and `HttpParserSettings`. The table owns nothing and holds no context, so
it is a plain value, `CZeroable` (every slot NULL); its constructor, `llhttp_settings_init`
(an `init` constructor, submitted to the ownership store with the 23 slots' pointer
findings), is `Settings::new` and `Default`, bound with the type as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has it; wave 195's port of `fn::llhttp_settings_init` replaces it. Each of
the 23 slots has a getter on `SettingsRef`, returning `Option<Callback>` or
`Option<DataCallback>`, and a setter on `SettingsMut` taking one, the slot's anchor on both,
so that 46 accessors stand in for the 23 fields. `Debug` lists the slots that are set.

What a table may hold (`crustify/evolution/callback-context-in-an-argument`, which this batch
weighed): a slot is set only from batch 1's callable types, whose C half `from_fn` accepts
only a function sound with any parser whatever its `data` holds, so every table Rust builds
is sound with every parser. The handles' invariant is that every non-NULL slot is such a
function, which the getters rely on to rebuild the callable (`Callback::from_fn`, no longer
dead code), and which a handle `from_ptr` builds over a C table vouches for. libgit2's own C
callbacks read `parser->data` as their `http_parser_context`, so they are no `Callback` and
their table is no `Settings` Rust can build: C installs it, or `ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`,
whose contract carries the parser's `data`, and its callbacks are reached only through the
parser that holds it, by api.c's dispatchers (`CALLBACK_MAYBE`, wave 195). The proposal
records the decision and the `binding-symbols` wording it suggests; the spec change is not
made.

With the table bound, `fld::llhttp__internal_s.settings` gains the typed setter batch 0 left
raw, `ParserMut::set_settings(Option<SettingsRef<'static>>)`, safe: the parser keeps the
table's address wherever it moves, and a `'static` shared handle neither moves, changes nor
goes. A `static` holds a table through `LazyLock`, since `Settings` is `Send` and `Sync`
(the two asserted impls the safety audit counts): its slots are function pointers read only
through a shared borrow, and C never writes a table it is given. Its getter stays the raw
`settings_ptr`, by the same judgement: a `SettingsRef` read back from a parser C initialised
would hand out its callbacks as callable with any parser. The setter took `&'static
Settings` until ffimap's first scan counted it a reference to a cell (`&cell +1`); the
handle gives the same guarantee and keeps the convention. The raw bindings gain
`llhttp_finish` and `llhttp_reset`, which the equivalence tests call.

Tests: 16 `unit_pub` (the empty table, every setter against its getter alone and with the
others set, `None` clearing, a slot read back and called, the typedefs, `Send` and `Sync`,
the setter's address and `None`, the slots a response and a chunked request with a
following message run, in order, `on_headers_complete`'s `1`, `2` and `-1`, a data slot's
`-1` as `HPE_USER` with api.c's reason, a pause, `reinit` clearing the table), 7 `ub_safe`
(handles alternating over a zeroed table and tables in a growing `Vec`; eight threads sharing a
`static` table, each with its own parser; a parser holding a table moved between runs;

- **contracts**: `ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`'s `# Safety` did not say how long a reason its
  callbacks set must live, though llhttp lets a callback set any string
  (`llhttp_set_error_reason`), and the safe `ParserRef::reason` follows it at any later time. A
  reproducer that keeps to both `unsafe` setters' contracts sets a reason its context owns, frees
  the context once the parser is done, and then reads freed memory through `reason()` (ASan
  heap-use-after-free). The contract now asks that such a reason stay live and unchanged while
  the parser holds it, and `Callback::from_fn`'s that a reason its function sets live as long as
  the program. `reason`'s `SAFETY` comment and the module documentation name both. The
  regression test is `ub_unsafe`'s
  `set_settings_ptr::a_reason_its_callbacks_set_is_read_while_the_parser_holds_it`.

What held. `set_settings(Option<SettingsRef<'static>>)` did not break. A local table and a leaked
`&'static mut` written afterwards are refused at compile time (batch 2's compile-fail
doctests), a `Mutex` guard lends its table only for the guard's borrow, and a table replaced or
cleared mid-parse is sound (batch 2's `ub_safe` tests). C reads a table only through `const llhttp_settings_t *`
(`api.c`'s `CALLBACK_MAYBE`, `llhttp_reset`). `Settings`' `Send` and `Sync` hold, since its slots
are `Callback` and `DataCallback` function pointers and nothing writes it through a shared
borrow. `data` and the `settings` getter stay raw addresses with good reason: a handle may
address a parser whose table C built, whose callbacks read `data` as their context. So a safe
`set_data`, or a `SettingsRef` read back from a parser, would hand C a context it does not expect.
The cost is that a Rust handler reaches per-parser context only through `unsafe` or a
thread-local; no primitive expresses a context reached through an argument yet. The six
private fields without an accessor are touched by `llhttp.c`'s generated code alone. A grep
of `api.c`, `http.c`, `transports/httpclient.c`, `httpparser.c`/`.h` and the C tests confirms

# A callback can re-enter the function that calls it, through the object it is handed

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A rule the how-to skills lack, which a binding had to work out by hand (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section has a trampoline refuse "a re-entrant call,
which would alias an `FnMut` closure": the hazard it names is the closure's state. It says
nothing of the function that runs the callback, whose own state the callback can reach when
C hands it the object the function is working on. Re-entering that function, or resetting
the object, from the callback is then undefined behaviour in C, reachable from safe Rust.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s `llhttp__internal_execute`, bound as
`ParserMut::parse`). The parser's settings name callbacks C calls with the parser being
parsed, so a Rust handler receives that parser's exclusive handle, from which a safe API
offers `parse` and `reinit`. A nested `llhttp__internal_execute` on the same parser sets
`_span_pos0` into the nested input and moves `_index`; the outer run, resuming after the
callback, then hands a span callback `(state->_span_pos0, p)` across two allocations (a
wild length), and `llparse__match_sequence*` index their blobs with the nested `_index`.
`llhttp__internal_init` from a callback nulls `_span_pos0`, which a span-end state reads
back as its start. The batch refuses both with a panic, through a thread-local register of
the parsers each thread is executing, which the trampolines' barrier turns into the
callback's error (`tests/ub_unsafe/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`,
`a_handler_cannot_parse_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`,
`a_handler_cannot_initialise_the_parser_whose_parse_runs_it`).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols`, Function pointers, beside the trampoline's re-entry rule; and
`analysis`' Findings, which should list it as something the analysis establishes.

## Change

Not made yet. In `binding-symbols` § Function pointers, after the paragraph on the
trampoline's re-entry refusal:

> A function that calls a callback with an object it is working on lends that object to
> the callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from
> within the callback; a routine it does not, the function itself or one that resets the
> state the function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, on the thread that
> runs the function, since the callback holds an exclusive handle the borrow checker
> cannot tell from any other.

In `analysis` § Findings, under states and transitions: "the calls a callback may make on
the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state".

## Validation

None run: the rule is the one this batch followed; a rerun of the batch under it would
produce the same binding. The batch's two UB tests above, run under ASan+UBSan, Miri (they
stop at the foreign call) and BSan alone, are its evidence that the refusal holds.

## Review

None yet.
# An export whose C declaration no header holds has no raw binding to be checked against

Status: `open` (the workaround `wave-194/batch-4/run-1` took; the spec change is not made).

## Signal

A rule an agent works around (`evolution` §2). `testing-gates`' Regressions section has a
`port` batch check "each export … at compile time against the raw binding of the C
declaration it replaces", and `export-signature-check` (crustify `dfd557c`, awaiting review)
has the binding "allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it". `bindgen`'s Extending
section lets a batch add to `wrapper.h` only "an internal header … when one of them is
declared there". Neither covers a function the remaining C calls through a prototype it
writes in its own translation unit, which no header holds: bindgen never sees it, so it
has no raw binding, the export cannot be checked against one, and an equivalence test cannot
call its C through one.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-4/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/api.c`, symbol route). api.c defines 23 dispatchers,
`int llhttp__on_<slot>(llhttp_t* s, const char* p, const char* endp)`, which `llhttp.c`'s
generated parser calls through prototypes it declares itself, `int
llhttp__on_<slot>(llhttp__internal_t* s, const unsigned char* p, const unsigned char*
endp);` (`c/deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`, lines 569–1144); `llhttp.h` declares none of them. The
batch exported all 23 under `ffi-export-deps-llhttp-api-c` and

- checked each against a function-pointer type written by hand in the gateway from
  `llhttp.c`'s prototype (`type Dispatcher = unsafe extern "C" fn(*mut
  sys::llhttp__internal_t, *const c_uchar, *const c_uchar) -> c_int;`, then `let _:
  Dispatcher = llhttp__on_url;` per export, `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`), which catches
  an export that drifts from the others but not from C, since the type is the batch's own
  transcription; and
- compared the Rust dispatchers with api.c's in `tests/equiv/deps/llhttp/api.rs` through an
  `unsafe extern "C"` block of the 23 prototypes, written by hand in the test, outside the
  raw bindings.

## Destination

The spec: `bindgen`'s Extending section, and `porting-symbols`' Functions section, which
the translator's role evolves, where `export-signature-check` describes the check.

## Change

Not made: it touches `bindgen`'s layout, which is not the translator's, and wants its own
review. Two candidates:

- each link unit's bindings gain a hand-written header, `sys/<link-unit>/declarations.h`,
  included by `wrapper.h`, that holds a copy of each prototype the remaining C declares only
  in a translation unit, with the file and line it copies, for the functions a batch exports
  or compares; the allowlist then reaches them as any other function, the export is checked
  against that binding, and the header loses each prototype with the export's
  `port/unexport`; or
- `porting-symbols` states the workaround as the rule: the export is checked against a
  function-pointer type transcribed beside the gateway from the caller's prototype, citing
  it, and an equivalence test declares the C it calls in an `extern` block of its own,
  citing the same.

The first keeps the check against C's own text, which a C change to the prototype would
break at the next regeneration, as the rule intends; the second needs nothing new but
checks only a transcription. The first is recommended.

## Validation

None run.

# A function that is one field's read or write is ported onto that field's accessor

Status: `open` (the rule `wave-194/batch-3/run-1` followed; the spec change is not made).

## Signal

A case the how-to skills leave unspecified, which a port had to settle by hand (`evolution`
§2). `porting-symbols`' Functions section gives a ported function "the safe API
`binding-symbols`' Functions section gives a function", homed in the file its item names,
and the conventions' Anchors section allows one Rust item to stand in for several C items
only for a symbol alias and for the accessors of one field. Neither says what a port does
with a function whose whole body reads or writes one member of a struct whose layout is
already bound, with an accessor for that member, in another module's file: a new method
in the function's own home duplicates the accessor, and annotating the accessor puts the
function's anchor outside its home.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-3/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/api.c`, symbol route). Nine of api.c's functions,
`llhttp_get_type`, `llhttp_get_http_major`, `llhttp_get_http_minor`, `llhttp_get_method`,
`llhttp_get_status_code`, `llhttp_get_upgrade`, `llhttp_get_errno`,
`llhttp_get_error_reason` and `llhttp_get_error_pos`, are `return parser-><field>;`, and
`llhttp_set_error_reason` is `parser->reason = reason;`. `deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`
(`llhttp.c`'s file, wave-194/batch-0) already has `ParserRef::parser_type`, `http_major`,
… `reason`, `error_offset` and `ParserMut::set_reason` over those members. The three
X-macro generators `HTTP_ERRNO_GEN`, `HTTP_METHOD_GEN` and `HTTP_STATUS_GEN`, each `case
PREFIX##NAME: return <text>;`, are batch 1's `Errno::constant_name`, `Method::map_string`
and `Status::map_string`. The batch's task message asked for these to be ported "as the
parser's native API, without duplicating what `llhttp.rs` gives": the batch added each
function's `Replaces` anchor and alias to the existing accessor beside the member's
`Wraps` one, so that 13 of its 28 items stand in through items in `llhttp.rs`, not in
their home `api.rs`, and wrote native code only for the items with logic of their own
(`execute`, `pause`, the resumptions, the lenient setters, `debug_trace`).

`wave-194/batch-4/run-1` met the case again with three functions whose whole body is a map's
text: `llhttp_errno_name`, `llhttp_method_name` and `llhttp_status_name` are each a `switch` of
the `case`s `HTTP_ERRNO_GEN`, `HTTP_METHOD_GEN` and `HTTP_STATUS_GEN` make, with a `default:
abort();` no Rust enum reaches. It ported them as `Errno::constant_name`, `Method::map_string`
and `Status::map_string`, which now carry a third anchor each (the map's, the generator's and
the function's), in `llhttp.rs`, as batch 3 did for the generators. So the rule should also
cover a function whose body only maps an enum's value to what an existing item of the safe API
already returns for it, and say that a third or later anchor on one item is expected.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols` § Functions (the translator's to evolve), and the
conventions' Anchors § Several stand-ins, which should name the case.

## Change

Not made: no review run was available to this batch. In `porting-symbols` § Functions,
after the first paragraph:

> A function whose body only reads or writes one member, or returns a value an existing
> item of the safe API already gives, is ported as that item: the accessor or method
> carries the function's `Replaces` anchor and alias beside its own, wherever it is
> homed, and the port writes no second API. Its export, where remaining C calls it, is
> written in its own module's gateway, over that item.

And in the conventions' § 3.2, beside the symbol alias: "and the existing accessor or
method a ported function is, as `porting-symbols`' Functions section describes".

## Validation

None run: the rule is the one this batch followed; a rerun under it would produce the
same port.

None yet.

2://!
3://! # The settings
4://!
5://! A [`Settings`] is llhttp's table of callbacks, `struct llhttp_settings_s`, which
6://! `llhttp.h` also names `llhttp_settings_t` and libgit2's `transports/httpparser.h`
7://! `git_http_parser_settings` ([`SettingsT`], [`HttpParserSettings`]). It has a slot per event
8://! of a message, each NULL or a callback: a [`Callback`] for an event, such as the start of a
9://! message or the end of its headers, and a [`DataCallback`] for a run of the input that makes
10://! up a part of it, such as a header's name or the body. A parser keeps the address of the table
11://! it is given (`llhttp_init`, [`ParserMut::set_settings`]), and api.c's dispatchers read the
12://! table on every event of a parse, calling the slot's callback with the parser, or nothing when
13://! the slot is NULL.
14://!
15://! The table owns nothing and holds no context: llhttp's callbacks are handed the parser, whose
16://! `data` is their context. It keeps its C layout until its `port/layout` stage, since libgit2's
17://! HTTP client builds one in C, a `static` filled on first use, and hands it to `llhttp_init`.
18://! A table Rust holds is a plain value, built empty by [`Settings::new`] (`llhttp_settings_init`)
19://! and filled through [`SettingsMut`]'s setters, one per slot; [`SettingsRef`]'s getters read
20://! the slots back as the callable types.
21://!
22://! # What a table may hold
23://!
24://! Each slot is set only from a [`Callback`] or a [`DataCallback`]: a Rust handler behind its
25://! trampoline, or, inside the crate, a C function that is sound to call with any parser, whatever
26://! its `data` holds. So every callback of a table Rust builds is sound with every parser, and a
27://! table installed with [`ParserMut::set_settings`] needs no promise about the parser's `data`:
28://! that setter is safe, taking a `SettingsRef<'static>`, whose table lives and stays unchanged for
29://! as long as any parser can keep its address.
30://!
31://! A C callback that reads its context through the parser's `data`, as each of libgit2's HTTP
32://! client's does with its `http_parser_context`, is sound only with the parsers whose `data` it
33://! expects, so it is no `Callback`, and a table of them is no `Settings` Rust can build. Such a
34://! table is installed by C, or through the `unsafe` [`ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`], whose caller
35://! vouches for the parser's `data`, and its callbacks are reached only through the parser that
36://! holds it, by api.c's dispatchers. That is why the parser's `settings` is read back as the
37://! address it holds ([`ParserRef::settings_ptr`]), not as a [`SettingsRef`], whose getters
38://! hand out callbacks callable with any parser.
39://!
40://!
41://! # The parser's API
42://!
43://! api.c's functions over a parser are methods of its handles, [`ParserRef`] and
44://! [`ParserMut`]. Most of them read or write one field, and are that field's accessor in
45://! `llhttp.rs`, which stands in for both: `llhttp_get_type`, `llhttp_get_method` and
46://! `llhttp_get_errno` are [`ParserRef::parser_type`], [`ParserRef::method`] and
47://! [`ParserRef::error`], read as llhttp's enums; `llhttp_get_http_major`,
48://! `llhttp_get_http_minor`, `llhttp_get_status_code` and `llhttp_get_upgrade` are
49://! [`ParserRef::http_major`], [`ParserRef::http_minor`], [`ParserRef::status_code`] and
50://! [`ParserRef::upgrade`]; `llhttp_get_error_reason` and `llhttp_set_error_reason` are
51://! [`ParserRef::reason`] and [`ParserMut::set_reason`]; and `llhttp_get_error_pos`, whose
52://! pointer into a past input Rust never follows, is [`ParserRef::error_offset`], which
53://! locates it in the input it is given. The X-macro generators api.c's name functions
54://! expand, `HTTP_ERRNO_GEN`, `HTTP_METHOD_GEN` and `HTTP_STATUS_GEN`, turn a map's entry into
55://! the text its `case` returns, which is [`Errno::constant_name`], [`Method::map_string`]
56://! and [`Status::map_string`].
57://!
58://! What has logic of its own is here: [`ParserMut::execute`] (`llhttp_execute`), the
59://! pause and its two resumptions ([`ParserMut::pause`], [`ParserMut::resume`],
60://! [`ParserMut::resume_after_upgrade`]), which move the parser between its running and
61://! paused states only from the state each expects, the ten lenient setters, each of which
62://! sets or clears one bit of the lenient flags, and [`ParserRef::debug_trace`]
63://! (`llhttp__debug`), the trace llhttp's generated parser writes to C's `stderr` when it is
64://! generated in debug mode, which this build's is not. The parser's lifecycle is here too:
65://! [`ParserMut::init`] (`llhttp_init`) starts it afresh with a type and a table,
66://! [`ParserMut::reset`] (`llhttp_reset`) starts it afresh between two connections' messages,
67://! keeping its type, table, `data` and lenient flags, and [`ParserMut::finish`]
68://! (`llhttp_finish`) tells it the input has ended. The name functions `llhttp_errno_name`,
69://! `llhttp_method_name` and `llhttp_status_name` are the maps' [`Errno::constant_name`],
70://! [`Method::map_string`] and [`Status::map_string`], whose `abort` on a value no entry names
71://! an enum cannot reach.
72://!
73://! # The dispatchers
74://!
75://! llhttp's generated parser signals each event of a message through one of api.c's 23
76://! dispatchers, `llhttp__on_<slot>`, which call the slot of the parser's table of the same
77://! name with the parser, or return `0` when the parser has no table or the slot is NULL. The
78://! macro `CALLBACK_MAYBE` makes the 14 that signal an event, such as
79://! [`ParserMut::on_message_begin`], and `SPAN_CALLBACK_MAYBE` the 9 that hand over a run of the
80://! input, such as [`ParserMut::on_url`], which also turn the callback's `-1` into `HPE_USER`,
81://! with the reason `"Span callback error in <slot>"`. They are the parser's methods of the
82://! same name, each over one of two private functions that stand in for the macros.

85://! read the parser's `data` as their context: they reach it through the parser alone, so
86://! that each callback is called only with the parser whose table holds it, as the contracts
87://! of [`ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`] and [`ParserMut::set_data`] promise it may be.
88://!

92://! `transports/httpparser.c` calls `llhttp_execute`, `llhttp_finish`, `llhttp_get_error_pos`

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total
